More Trials, Better Trials, or More Tasks?

Simulation Insights for Accuracy Measures of Cognitive Individual Differences

Han Hao

October 2026 - Brown Bag Sesssion 1

Background & Motivation

The measurement issue in individual differences research and the need of updated task designing in cognitive ToM.

Individual differences Investigations

It usually starts from an experimental task (group/condition-level differences) to a person measure

  • A cognitive task shows an experimental or quasi-experimental effect where people performed differently across different conditions.

  • The conditions are designed and manipulated to engage different cognitive processes, or reflect different cognitive behaviors.

  • We now want to use such task performance to rank people on a target cognitive ability.

Some (related) decisions due to the behavioral research limitations

  1. Which cognitive process(es) are we really measuring?
  2. Which responses should count toward the score to represent individual differences reliably and validly?
  3. How should we distribute trials (to different conditions) and the tasks (in different paradigms and/or in different stimuli)?

A robust condition difference need not give stable person rankings

Experimental question

Do people’s average performance in one condition differ from the other on average?

Individual-differences question

Does a person’s score preserve a reproducible meaning reflecting their standings on certain “process”?

Hedge et al. tested RT and error difference measures in seven classic cognitive tasks. Test–retest ICCs were generally poor.

A dependable group effect and a dependable person measure require different evidence.

Hedge, Powell, & Sumner (2018), The reliability paradox.

Repeating the same mixture can be very “reliable”

But does a reliable task really guarantee a solution to individual differences precision?

Reliability/Repeatability

Would the same people receive similar scores again?

Validity/Process recovery

Do those scores track the intended ability?

Si=Ti+Mi+ei S_i = T_i + M_i + e_i

  • TT: intended process
  • MM: stable additional demand (?)
  • ee: response noise

More trials can reduce response noise while preserving stable method/domain/paradigm influences.

Trait–method distinction: Campbell & Fiske (1959), multitrait–multimethod validation.

Quick example

A cognitive task intended to measure some core ability, e.g., memory retention, but also requires language comprehension (to read the materials).

  • Both the exact paradigm and the required “extra” abilities will bring in stable impact to the performance.
  • High reliability does not guarantee construct validity. If language ability is stable, repeated scores may consistently reflect both Core and language ability.

Task Score=Memory+Language+Paradigm+Error \text{Task Score}=\text{Memory}+\text{Language}+\text{Paradigm}+\text{Error}

Potential measurement solutions

Difference scoring based on the experimental design thinking

  • include a parallel task/condition with the same paradigm and stimuli, but don’t require “memory retention” (serving as the Control), subtracting the scores across the two versions to find a “pure” score of “memory retention”.

  • The E–C contrast has a clear experimental rationale. Its person-level interpretation still depends on what both conditions require.

Multiple-task setup based on psychometrics thinking

  • design memory tasks with paradigms and/or use stimuli that rely on different “extra” abilities, aggregate the scores to cancel the “unwanted components” out.

  • The multiple-task setup has a clear psychometrics rationale. But people need to design and administer 2 or more task paradigms.

Attention control: shared demands and extra conflict

Some attention control measures applied the first solution.

Issues

  • Low reliability of the difference score measures (accuracy or RT).
  • Common and specific abilities coexist in cognitive performance: A task (regardless the scoring approach) can reflect a common ability while retaining domain-specific requirements.

Why subtraction is appealing and what it assumes

Ideal additive case

Ei=Ti+Ni,Ci=Ni,soEi−Ci=Ti E_i = T_i + N_i,\qquad C_i = N_i,\qquad so \qquad E_i-C_i=T_i

The shared contribution NN cancels if it contributes to E & C in the same and additive way.

Questions for actual accuracy data

  • Does C also engage the target process to some extent?
  • Do processes really work additively, or can one become a bottleneck, a multiplier, or even a “log base” of the other?
  • How much response uncertainty enters both estimated accuracies?

Working memory: one label, different requirements

Working memory capacity measures typically apply the 2nd solution (verbal, numerical, visuospatial, etc.).

Construct validity across task paradigms may still have some issues

Various findings have indicated that n-back and operation span correlated only weakly to moderately, while each explained independent variation in fluid intelligence.

Intelligence batteries covering different broad abilities by aggregating narrow ability performances

A precise measure of one domain may support a narrow inference. A broad inference also needs justified coverage for core/target ability estimation.

Theory of mind: from experimental to individual differences

what makes an answer correct DT task? And does it a reflection of individual differences in perspective taking?

A correct choice in DT can depend on perspective use, selecting among objects, and understanding the instruction. But how?

Empirical errors do not map neatly onto one process

For example, Legg et al. (2017) compared perspective-taking with a matched rule task.

Task Mean error rate on experimental trials
Level 1 perspective-taking 16.7%
Level 2 perspective-taking 10.0%
Rule following 3.9%

Requiring perspective-taking affected errors; greater perspective complexity did not produce the predicted significant increase.

Level 1 and Level 2 error rates were not significantly different, while both significantly different from the control (Rule-following).

Simulation to investigate

  • Generating subjects with pure cognitive process scores representing real human individual differences in cognition.

  • Applying certain algorithms to mimic potential cognitive mechanisms of human responding behavioral stimuli.

  • Scoring and analyzing these behavioral-level responses and comparing them with the “true” cognitive process scores.

  • Comparing the resulting situations across scoring approaches, task “designs”, and even different algorithms representing certain cognitive mechanism hypotheses.

Current Simulation Algorithms Overview

How the people, tasks, and responses were generated

Simulating a process-mixture environment

Basic schema: three Type abilities share a core ability to different degrees, and each also has its own specific component. The type abilities are measured by different tasks in the same paradigm but with different stimulus format (verbal, numerical, spatial, etc.).

Arbitrary decisions: separate task Type from stimulus Format

Local definitions/terms Example interpretation Shared variation across tasks
Type Paradigm or subconstruct Core + Type-specific ability
Format Verbal, numerical, spatial material Format/stimuli-specific ability
Background General demands of doing the task Stable systematic additional ability

Simulating a crossed design of tasks, repeating each Type across all three Formats.

Two research questions for individual differences insights

Q1 · THE SCORING

Same task battery, different scoring methods

E+C, E−C, and E-only.

Which composite score is “better”? And whether estimated CFA factor scores help.

Q2 · THE ALLOCATION

Same # of total trials, different allocation

More Types, more tasks per Type, or more repetitive trials.

Use the scoring chosen in Q1 (for simplicity).

  • Better here means which condition contributes to better reliability and core ability estimation.
  • A systematic psychometric good-versus-bad item-task-quality comparison is reserved for future work.
  • A cross-design comparison (scoring approach by allocation setup) is possible but not included.

Simulating people before simulating tasks

We simulate each person’s Core, Type, Format, and Background ability standings.

Based on these “true” standings, we can apply certain responding mechanisms (higher abilities have higher likelihood of accurate responses) to simulate individual’s task performance.

Known abilities→trial requirements→0/1 responses \text{Known abilities}\ \longrightarrow\ \text{trial requirements}\ \longrightarrow\ 0/1\text{ responses} We can ask whether an observed score or estimate recovers those known values (the true trait scores).

A single comparison across scoring approaches or allocations is within the same people. The next iteration draws a new “sample” of subjects.

Only accuracy indicators were considered in the current simulation design.

What stays the same and what changes across iterations?

Within one iteration of simulation Across the iterations in a full cycle
Same 200 people and stable ability standings New samples of 200 people each iteration
Same tasks in full edition (E and C trials) across 3 types and 3 formats Same full bank of 9 tasks but randomly selected for different allocations
Shared responses are reused across comparisons Fresh fluctuations and binary responses for each cohort

Think of one iteration as the new cohort doing all the same tasks and trials needed for different compared designs. The same task bank was used across iterations.

In each iteration, different scorings and allocations will select the completed trials and tasks from the full dataset.

If two scores use the same response, it is literally the same saved response in one iteration.

Build Core (target true) ability and Type abilities (paradigm/domain-biased core)

Gi,Ui1,Ui2,Ui3∼indN(0,1)G_i,\ U_{i1},U_{i2},U_{i3}\ \overset{\mathrm{ind}}{\sim}\ N(0,1)

Tik=λkGi+1−λk2UikT_{ik}=\lambda_k G_i+\sqrt{1-\lambda_k^2}\,U_{ik}

Type Link to Core, λk\lambda_k Type-specific variance
Type 1 .90 .1900
Type 2 .80 .3600

Type is loosely defined as subconstruct or (biased) core ability measured by a particular paradigm. Correlations between 3 types can be calculated by the lambda products: .72, .405, and .36.

One generated person has several standardized process scores

200 rows of process scores (ability standings) are generated and saved for an iteration. Process scores are used in combination with difficulty and discrimination parameters of trials in tasks, to generate binary accuracy responses.

Nine tasks, with one full task in each cell

One task per Type × Format cell. No extra task versions (same a and b parameters to generate responses across cohorts).

Each full task has 90 E + 90 C potential trials. The scoring comparison (section 1) uses the first 30 E + 30 C in every task. The allocation comparison (section 2) uses different numbers of trials depending on the exact allocation.

Section 1 administration: 3 Types × 3 tasks × 60 trials = 540 responses per person.

a and b parameters turn each process score into success

pigj=eagj(θig−bgj)1+eagj(θig−bgj)p_{igj} = \frac{e^{a_{gj}(\theta_{ig}-b_{gj})}}{1 + e^{a_{gj}(\theta_{ig}-b_{gj})}}

  • aa (discrimination) controls steepness and bb (difficulty) locates the requirement.
  • In this illustration: target a=1.35a=1.35, bE=−.8b_E=-.8, bC=−2.0b_C=-2.0.
  • Actual items have varying parameters for each required ability and are matched by type and format, and by each pair of E & C trials.

A weak required process can become the bottleneck

Noncompensatory across abilities (A very strict bottleneck rule)

pij*=min⁡{pBackground,pFormat,pType} p^*_{ij}=\min\{p_{\mathrm{Background}},p_{\mathrm{Format}},p_{\mathrm{Type}}\}

  • The minimum means that the least successful required component controls the baseline probability. This is a simple and very strict noncompensatory mechanism.

  • A strong process cannot rescue a weak required process. It is not necessarily how things work in reality.

Momentary fluctuation and a binary response: Added for “reliability” estimation

qij=min⁡{1,max⁡(0,pij*+.10zij)},zij∼N(0,1)q_{ij}=\min\{1,\max(0,p^*_{ij}+.10z_{ij})\}, \quad z_{ij}\sim N(0,1) Yij∼Bernoulli⁡(qij)Y_{ij}\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(q_{ij})

What counts as successful measurement?

Question Statistic in this simulation
Recover the core ability? r(Si,Gi)r(S_i,G_i)
Recover each measured Type? Mean of r(Sik,Tik)r(S_{ik},T_{ik}) across measured Types
Reproduce person scores? r(Si(1),Si(2))r(S_i^{(1)},S_i^{(2)}) *
Retain other process influences? Background, random flunctuation that are not designed, etc.

Compute each correlation within a 200-person cohort, then summarize the point estimates across cohorts.

*Reliability (repeatbility) in the simulation was calculated by regenerating a full set of responses for unchanged people and items. It is not an empirical test–retest reliability estimate, I actually “asked” the same people to do the same tasks twice.

Section 1a: Why subtraction is not a pure target score here

I did not simulate the cognitive engagement in an additive fashion: Both E and C trials still engage the target in some way; C makes that requirement easier. It changes the meaning of a simple subtraction.

Specifically, I did a non-compensatory, bottleneck design.

Illustration: for two people with the same fix target success at E = .70, C = .90 but different background ability.

Background success E probability C probability E−C
.50 — limits both conditions .50 .50 .00
.95 — target becomes limiting .70 .90 −.20
The difference changes with Background even when the target is unchanged.

Nine task composites (3 scoring approaches) → three first-order Type factors → high-order Core.

Continuous linear CFA, MLR estimation.

Section 2: If we have a fixed budget, how should we allocate the tasks?

How do we collect the data on 270 trials to estimate the target ability precisely?

Battery Types Tasks per Type E trials per task Total
Broad coverage, short tasks 3 3 30 270
Moderate coverage, long tasks 3 1 90 270
One type, three tasks 1 3 90 270
One really long task 1 1 × 3 times 90 270

All use E-only based on the results from Section 1a; no C trials are administered in Section 2.

Section 2: Broad coverage recovers core ability better on average

The moderate coverage with long tasks is also not bad.

The unstable performance of the later two allocations were due to the lower correlation of Type 3 to the core ability. If your paradigm is more domain-specific, there will be issues with narrow coverage.

Again, Error bars were 10th–90th percentiles (across all the point estimates).

Section 2: A one-Type battery can be stable and recover that Type

More trials refines within Type; they do not erase its specificity.

Discussion, Limitation, & Future Direction

For this ongoing simulation project…

“Old folk tales” generally reassured

  1. Reliability and validity, and operational definitions with task paradigms. A stable score can consistently retain other abilities.
  2. The utility of difference score is questionable, depending on the applicability of additive effects. Its value depends on shared processes, how they combine, and response precision.
  3. Be cautious of what you are measuring: Match coverage to the intended construct. More trials may not be better than more tasks.
Define the intended inference first, then operationalized definition of constructs, then justify the tasks, conditions, scoring, and/or latent variable model.

What remains uncertain and what to test next

Current assumptions

  • Minimum-probability rule: a bucket-effect type of non-compensatory mechanism

  • Independent trial fluctuations (from person, from background, etc.)

  • Static process scores, 2PL response generation, and matched item parameters.

Future extensions

  • C with no potential target process demand at all.

  • Other potential compensatory mechanism of process engagement.

  • RT vs. Accuracy, DDT-based data generation (?)

Questions of our (my?) time

What can we improve now in the measurement of cognitive individual differences?

  • Moderate(?)-hanging fruit: task design, scoring, better psychometric modeling, transparent validity inspections.

  • Harder question: are some limits of cognitive mechanisms really approachable via conventional, simple models on behavioral measures, or are they not “modelable” given the nature of complex behavior as complex system?
